name: Apomorphine

what.text: Apomorphine is a dopamine agonist: it stimulates the brain's dopamine receptors. In the US it is approved for Parkinson's disease as injections (Apokyn, Onapgo). A film under the tongue, Kynmobi, was approved in 2020 and is now listed as discontinued. In the EU it was authorised for erectile dysfunction (ED) in 2001 as Uprima, Ixense and Taluvian; all three authorisations have since ended.

items.text: The Apokyn label says it binds strongly to the dopamine D4 receptor and moderately to D2, D3 and D5 receptors and some adrenergic receptors. Its effect in Parkinson's is thought to come from D2-type receptors in the brain.
For ED, it was studied as a drug acting in the brain rather than in penile blood vessels. The EMA records say sexual stimulation was needed for Uprima to have an effect.

items.text: Injected under the skin, apomorphine has a half-life of about 40 minutes.

research.text: Sublingual apomorphine (under the tongue) was tested for ED in randomized, placebo-controlled trials of 4 to 8 weeks around 2000. A 2020 systematic review included nine of them. In the one head-to-head trial with sildenafil reviewed here, sildenafil did better. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no registered study of apomorphine for ED.

research.title: First sublingual formulations (Urology 1995)

facts.v: Heaton JP, Morales A, Adams MA, et al. Urology 1995;45(2):200-6
four preliminary protocols, compared with placebo, with erections measured on a RigiScan
men with ED and no measurable physical cause (for example 10 evaluable men in one protocol, 12 in another)
sublingual liquid, a 5 mg tablet, a nasal spray, and new 3 and 4 mg controlled-absorption tablets
erection response during erotic or neutral video; home use

research.found: 7 of 10 responded to the liquid, but most had significant nausea. With the 3 and 4 mg tablets, 8 of 12 men (67%) had erections and 7 of 11 kept using it at home. The authors note apomorphine had already been reported to cause erections in animals and men when injected.

research.title: Fixed and adjusted doses (Urology 2000)

facts.v: Dula E, Keating W, Siami PF, et al.; Apomorphine Study Group. Urology 2000;56(1):130-5
multicenter, double-blind, four groups
569 men with ED
sublingual apomorphine starting at 2 mg and adjusted, fixed 5 mg, fixed 6 mg, or placebo
8 weeks
home questionnaires from men and partners, the IIEF and the Brief Sexual Function Inventory

research.found: 48% to 53% of men on apomorphine had an erection firm enough for intercourse, vs 35% on placebo (P ≤ 0.001). 45% to 51% of attempts led to intercourse, vs 33%. Nausea was the most common side effect; it rose with dose and fell in the second 4 weeks.

research.title: Apomorphine 3 mg vs sildenafil 50 mg (J Urol 2004)

facts.v: Pavone C, Curto F, Anello G, et al. J Urol 2004;172(6 Pt 1):2347-9
prospective, randomized crossover with a 4-week washout; no placebo
77 men enrolled, 62 randomized, 34 evaluable
sublingual apomorphine 3 mg or oral sildenafil 50 mg
4 weeks on each drug
share of attempts with an erection firm enough for intercourse; IIEF

research.found: Erections firm enough for intercourse followed 44% of attempts on apomorphine and 85% on sildenafil (P < 0.0001). Side-effect rates did not differ significantly. Fewer than half the men enrolled were evaluable.

src.label: Pavone et al., J Urol, PubMed

research.title: Nine placebo-controlled trials (Arch Sex Behav 2020)

facts.v: Guillén V, Rueda JR, Lopez-Argumedo M, et al. Arch Sex Behav 2020;49(8):2963-79
systematic review of randomized controlled trials; search ended January 9, 2019
9 trials of men with ED
sublingual apomorphine 2 to 6 mg vs placebo
trials lasted 4 to 8 weeks
share of successful intercourse attempts; erectile function scores; stopping for side effects

research.found: Trials found 6% to 27% more successful attempts than placebo; in one trial after prostate removal, the difference was not significant. In trials limited to men with diabetes or after prostate removal, score differences were not clinically relevant. More men stopped for side effects on apomorphine, especially at higher doses.

us.text: Apomorphine is FDA approved, by prescription, for Parkinson's disease as Apokyn injection (2004) and Onapgo infusion (2025). Kynmobi, a film under the tongue approved in 2020, is listed as discontinued. Apomorphine has never been approved for ED in the US, so use for ED is off-label. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: approved April 20, 2004 (NDA 021264) as a new molecular entity, with priority review. Approved use: on-demand treatment of "off" episodes in advanced Parkinson's disease. Generic apomorphine injection was approved in 2022.
a film placed under the tongue, approved May 21, 2020 (NDA 210875). FDA's data list every Kynmobi strength as discontinued, and the search found no current Kynmobi label on DailyMed.
a continuous infusion under the skin, approved February 3, 2025 (NDA 214056) for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson's disease.
no FDA-approved apomorphine product lists ED as a use. The sublingual tablets authorised in Europe for ED (Uprima, Ixense, Taluvian) have no US approval in FDA's data.
the Apokyn label says it must not be used with 5HT3-blocking anti-nausea drugs such as ondansetron, because of reports of profound low blood pressure and loss of consciousness.

us.text: FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA approved, which means FDA does not verify their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.

world.lead: Apomorphine is approved for Parkinson's disease in the US and Australia, and authorised nationally in EU countries such as Ireland. The EU's three ED authorisations (Uprima, Ixense, Taluvian, 2001) were withdrawn or expired by 2006. Canada lists no current human apomorphine product. It is not on WADA's Prohibited List.

countries.status: Approved medicine for Parkinson's disease (Apokyn 2004; Onapgo 2025). Kynmobi (2020) is listed as discontinued. Never approved for ED. Prescription-only.
No current human product: Movapo injection and Kynmobi film were both cancelled after marketing in 2023. The only other current listing is a veterinary product.

ED: Uprima, Ixense and Taluvian were authorised EU-wide on May 28, 2001. Taluvian and Ixense were withdrawn in 2004 and Uprima expired on May 28, 2006, all for commercial reasons. Apomorphine injections (APO-go, Dacepton) are authorised nationally in Ireland.

countries.status: Approved medicine: TGA publishes product information for Apomine and Movapo apomorphine products. Prescription-only (Schedule 4).

after.text: European Union, ED history: EMA says Uprima was marketed in Ireland, the UK, Spain, France, Sweden and Norway; Ixense in Austria, Germany, France and Italy; and Taluvian only in Spain. The holders withdrew Taluvian and Ixense in 2004, and did not renew Uprima, citing commercial reasons. EMA's current list of centrally authorised medicines shows all three as withdrawn.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Apomorphine is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or on the 2027 List, which takes effect January 1, 2027. It is not in the 2027 Monitoring Program either. Class S0 covers only substances with no current government approval for human therapeutic use, and apomorphine is approved for some use (see above).

side.text: In the ED trials, nausea was the most common side effect and rose with dose. The Parkinson's labels list serious risks including fainting and low blood pressure, falling asleep suddenly, hallucinations, impulse-control problems, heart events and priapism.

items.text: nausea was the most common side effect of sublingual apomorphine and rose with dose. In the 2020 review, more men stopped for side effects on apomorphine than on placebo, especially at higher doses.

items.text: in Parkinson's studies, painful erections were reported by 3 of 361 men on Apokyn, and one man stopped because of priapism. The label says severe priapism may need surgery.
about 2% of Apokyn-treated patients fainted in clinical studies. Profound low blood pressure and loss of consciousness were reported with ondansetron, which is contraindicated.
patients on Apokyn have been reported to fall asleep suddenly, without warning, during daily activities. Sleepiness is common.
hallucinations were reported by 14% of Apokyn-treated patients in studies. Intense urges to gamble, spend money or have sex have been reported.
4% of Apokyn-treated patients in studies had angina, heart attack, cardiac arrest or sudden death. Apomorphine prolongs the QTc interval in a dose-related way.
hemolytic anemia needing hospital care, fibrotic complications, a fever-and-confusion syndrome on stopping, allergic reactions (it contains a sulfite), and dyskinesias.
yawning, sleepiness, dyskinesias, dizziness or low blood pressure on standing, runny nose, nausea or vomiting, hallucination or confusion, and swelling of the limbs.

surprises: Apomorphine was an authorised ED medicine across the EU from 2001, but all three EU authorisations ended by 2006 for commercial reasons, according to EMA.
Kynmobi, approved by FDA in 2020, is now listed as discontinued in FDA's data, and Health Canada cancelled its Kynmobi listings in 2023.
